questions.scenario: Rosa owns a 12-employee business in New York. For her small group health plan she is comparing two ACA metal-level plans from the same insurer: a Silver plan and a Gold plan.
questions.stem: What is the key difference between the two plans' metal levels?

choices.text: The Gold plan covers benefit categories that the Silver plan omits
choices.rationale: Incorrect: every metal-level plan provides the essential health benefits package; metal levels differ in cost-sharing, not in benefit categories.

choices.text: The Gold plan pays a larger average share of covered costs
choices.rationale: Correct: metal levels reflect actuarial value. A Gold plan pays about 80% of the costs of covered benefits for a standard population; Silver pays about 70%.

choices.text: The Silver plan is open only to employers with under 10 workers
choices.rationale: Incorrect: metal levels are not tied to employer size; small employers can choose any level the insurer offers.

choices.text: The Silver plan may leave out preventive and wellness services
choices.rationale: Incorrect: preventive and wellness services are one of the ten essential health benefit categories in every metal-level plan.

questions.explanation: Under 42 U.S.C. § 18022, an essential health benefits package covers the ten EHB categories and is offered at a level of coverage based on actuarial value: Bronze 60%, Silver 70%, Gold 80% and Platinum 90% of the full actuarial value of the benefits for a standard population. So the Gold and Silver plans cover the same categories of benefits; the Gold plan simply pays a larger average share of the cost (usually with a higher premium), leaving less cost-sharing for employees.
questions.memoryTip: 60-70-80-90: Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum. Same benefits, different cost split.

keyPoints.label: Metal levels reflect actuarial value / share of costs paid
Both cover the same essential health benefits
